# Hot-air and hydrogen balloons (`hot_air_hydrogen_balloon`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by gas_laws, sulphuric_acid, buoyancy_hydrostatics
- Core idea: A balloon floats because the gas inside is lighter than the air it displaces (Archimedes). At sea level, air heated from about 20 °C to 100 °C lifts roughly 0.25 kg per cubic metre, so a 1,000 m³ envelope of varnished linen or paper-lined silk lifts about 250 kg; hydrogen (from iron filings and sulphuric acid) lifts about 1.1 kg per cubic metre, four times more, but is explosive. It goes where the wind goes; height is controlled by heat or ballast and valving gas.
- Pitfalls:
  - Thinking smoke, not hot air, does the lifting (the Montgolfiers' own error)
  - Open fire under a hydrogen balloon
  - Expecting to steer it; without an engine it drifts with the wind
- History: china: unmanned paper sky lanterns (traditionally attributed to the 3rd c.; date uncertain); europe: 1709 – Bartolomeu de Gusmão demonstrates a small hot-air model in Lisbon; 4 June 1783 Montgolfier brothers' public ascent at Annonay; 21 Nov 1783 first manned flight (Pilâtre de Rozier and d'Arlandes); 1 Dec 1783 Charles and Robert's hydrogen balloon
- Read:
  - Charles Coulston Gillispie, The Montgolfier Brothers and the Invention of Aviation, 1783–1784 (1983)
  - Richard Holmes, Falling Upwards: How We Took to the Air (2013)
